displayQuote: The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another

meta.title: Who really said "The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — William James never wrote this. It appears in none of his works, and the word “stress” in this sense postdates his 1910 death by decades. A modern misattribution.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another'?
meta.ogDescription: No primary source, absent from Wikiquote, and “stress” in this sense didn’t exist in William James’s lifetime. An anachronistic modern misattribution.

answer.label: Not William James — an anachronistic modern misattribution
answer.sourceLine: This line is not found in any work by William James. It appears in none of his books, essays, or letters, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced and misattributed listings for him. The tell is the word “stress”: used in this psychological sense, the term only came into wide use from the 1930s–1950s (via Hans Selye), decades after James died in 1910. The broad idea — that we can choose which thought to hold — echoes James’s writing on will and attention, but this wording is a much later, source-less paraphrase pinned to his famous name.

source.heading: Where does it actually come from?

source.excerpt: The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another.
trail: Philosopher Jasper Reid, answering a reader on AskPhilosophers ↗, judges the attribution wrong: it “definitely doesn’t sound like William James, on account of the use of the word ‘stress’,” noting that stress in this sense “only really started to arise in the 1950s.”
The line is absent from Wikiquote’s William James page ↗ — it is in neither the sourced quotations nor the Misattributed section, i.e. no editor has been able to tie it to any James text.

Popular hubs repeat it with no citation: Goodreads ↗ carries only its notice that community quotes are “not verified,” and meaning-explainer pages like The Socratic Method ↗ analyse the sentiment while citing no primary source.
source.excerptNote: Endlessly reproduced on quote sites under William James’s name — always without a book, page, essay, or date.

author.name: William James
author.heading: About William James
author.metaLine: 1842–1910 · American philosopher & psychologist, “father of American psychology”
author.bio: William James (1842–1910) was an American philosopher and psychologist whose The Principles of Psychology (1890) helped found the discipline in the United States. He wrote extensively on will, attention, and habit — including the idea that the will’s essential act is to hold one object of thought before the mind — which is why glib “choose your thoughts” lines are so easily pinned to him. He did not, however, write the popular anti-stress sentence attributed here.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest documented as an uncited attribution to William James on quotation-aggregator sites; attribution challenged in Jasper Reid, response to “Is this a genuine William James quote?”, AskPhilosophers, question 5380.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to William James — no source in his works; an anonymous modern paraphrase.

misattribution.heading: How the misattribution works
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “famous-name magnet” quote: a tidy, self-help-friendly line about controlling your thoughts, glued onto the father of American psychology to lend it authority.

items.why: The sentence hinges on “stress” used as a modern psychological concept. As philosopher Jasper Reid notes on AskPhilosophers ↗, that sense of the word “only really started to arise in the 1950s” — James died in 1910, so it is unlikely to be his phrasing.
No book, essay, lecture, or letter is ever named. The line does not appear in Wikiquote’s sourced or misattributed sections ↗, and quote aggregators supply the name but never a source.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — that we can choose which thought to hold in mind — is broadly Jamesian, but this exact anti-“stress” sentence is a source-less modern paraphrase, as the attribution critique on AskPhilosophers ↗ makes clear.

context.heading: Why it sticks to his name
lead: James really did argue that attention and will let us select which idea occupies the mind — a genuinely appealing, empowering thought. A modern reader looking for a crisp motto about beating “stress” finds that this sentence feels like something he might have said, and his authority makes it more shareable. That resemblance is exactly what lets a source-less paraphrase pass as a quotation.
context.pull: The idea is Jamesian in spirit; the sentence is not James.
